text: The deal comes from a man he last saw in military service, and at first it is a good one. Fernando Ayala's comedy watches the money arrive faster than any account of where it came from: one day there is enough, the next there is more than enough, and nobody does the arithmetic aloud. Ninety-seven minutes, Argentina, 1982 — a place and a year in which a story about easy money was never going to be read as one man's private luck. The attention goes to manners rather than to the mechanics of the scheme: what a voice does once it can afford things, how a friendship made in uniform turns into a business relationship with terms attached. It took the Silver Condor for best film at home. The genre label says comedy. The punchline is bookkeeping.

The brothel district is where men without masters end up, and it is there that a militia arrives with a purpose. Ronin-gai hands its swordsmen no lord to serve and no cause worth the name; what it hands them instead is a street of women somebody has decided to be rid of, and the discovery that this is enough to fight about. The civil war is nearly finished, which makes these men obsolete in the eyes of everyone who counts, themselves included. Nearly two hours, made in Japan in 1928, and named the year's best film by Kinema Junpo. Honor is the word the ronin use for the thing they want back, and the film never defines it. It is busier with the interval — with what men do in the meantime, while they are waiting for a reason.

Allan King's camera spent five weeks inside a residential treatment centre near Toronto and was never once used to ask a question. Twelve emotionally disturbed children live there; adults are employed to look after them; that is the whole of the material, filmed in 1966 without commentary and without anyone being asked to do a thing twice. What emerges is less a series of events than a long practice of staying in the room. King later called the form actuality drama, and the phrase is exact. The shape comes from the days, not from an argument laid across them. A hundred and one minutes. The children are not case studies and the staff are not saints; they are people who were filmed at length by someone who had decided in advance not to interpret them.

A daughter needs her father home for a few days to perform the one office he still holds, which is the negotiation of her marriage. Kimiko earns her own living in a Tokyo office and lives with a mother who writes haiku and does not discuss the absence. Seventy-four minutes lets Mikio Naruse skip past everything except the errand and its cost, and the film turns when Kimiko finds her father settled with another woman and their children — a household that works, which is much harder to be angry at than one that does not. Nothing in the arrangement is scandalous on its own. It only requires that somebody travel out and ask. Kinema Junpo named it the best film of the year. The go-between everyone needs is the person who left.

The friendship is a three-part arrangement: a priest's daughter, a boy who prefers the forest to the schoolroom, and the gardener who joins in without taking over. Josefin is six, and her solitude in the countryside is a matter of geography and her father's occupation before it is a mood. Hugo arrives from wherever such boys arrive from, unbothered, apparently accountable to no one. Kjell Grede keeps the whole thing to eighty-two minutes and to the scale of what children actually do with an afternoon — invented rules, long detours, a seriousness the adult world files under play. Sweden's Guldbagge for best film went to it, which is a serious verdict on a picture whose main events are improvised by children. Very little occurs, and the film is confident that this is the correct amount.

The lie has a deadline: a brother is flying in from the United States expecting to meet the Jewish man his sister has let him believe in. Clara Goldstein places an advertisement and turns up Raul, who is well-spoken, agreeable, and the wrong faith entirely, so she sets about teaching him, at speed. Eduardo Mignogna gives a hundred and ten minutes to two people old enough to know precisely how this can go wrong and interested anyway, which is a different proposition from a film about the young finding each other. The premise is farce and the two people inside it are not the joke; what is being wagered is the last stretch of a life spent in company instead of alone. The Goya for best Ibero-American film went to it.

Half of the film is given to somebody who cannot yet speak in sentences. Kon Ichikawa alternates a not-quite-two-year-old's running assessment of the enormous people who carry him from room to room with the same run of days as his parents live them, a birthday coming up. Eighty-eight minutes, comedy and drama sharing every cut. The device could have stayed merely cute; what stops it is that the adults' half is never written down to the child's, so the two accounts run side by side with neither correcting the other. Kinema Junpo made it the best film of its year. The toddler is not a source of wisdom and not a symbol. He is a person working with incomplete information, which turns out to describe the grown-ups as well.

Two hours and eighteen minutes is a long time to give three children and one poor neighbourhood, and the length is the argument. What another film would compress into a montage of hardship is left running at the speed it actually happens: waiting, small negotiations conducted at knee height, the slow business of finding people who will have them. Shasha Nakhai follows kids who found each other somewhere nobody designed for them, and the adults nearby doing what the week's money allows. Toronto audiences voted it their favourite in 2021. No crisis is engineered to make the point; the children get to be funny, self-interested and easily distracted while the grown-up trouble goes on above their heads, and the film trusts accumulation to do the work a plot usually does.

A novel needs material, and Roberto finds his in the worst hour of a stranger's life. He sells insurance; the book has so far existed as an intention. Then Estela crosses his path on a day she had not expected to get through, and he begins, without ever calling it that, to take notes. Eliseo Subiela lets it run two hours and eleven minutes, unhurried, allowing the rescue and the appropriation to occupy the same gestures. The man is helping, and he is also collecting. Nothing in the film argues that these are different activities. A Silver Condor for best film came to it. Whether what Roberto does is monstrous or simply what every writer does is a question the film keeps open, and it stays open in a way that implicates whoever is watching.

The escape belongs to a seven-year-old, and nobody explains it to him. Matías comes back from a birthday party into a situation he has no word for, and from then on the city he grew up in is a run of rooms whose rules he has to infer: a shelter, an office, two nights somewhere, a decision taken over his head about where the rest of his life happens. Diego Lerman keeps the adult conversation at adult height. Ninety-five minutes, moving at the pulse of a thriller, because from down there that is what it is — a bus, a stranger's kindness and a locked door all arriving with the same weight, since he has no way to sort the danger from the getting away. His mother is making the decisions, and she is making them fast. He can only read the speed.

Daisuke is thirty and has never needed work, which his family can afford and everyone around him can only remark on. He reads, he listens to music, he absorbs the standing reminder that a respectable position and a respectable wife are still expected of him, and he treats all of it as weather. Then Hiraoka comes back with a wife, Michiyo, and the careful nothing Daisuke has built for himself stops holding. Two hours and ten minutes for a story with almost no incident: Yoshimitsu Morita lets scenes run well past the point where their information has been delivered. Kinema Junpo named it the best film of the year. Nothing external prevents Daisuke from taking the job and the wife. The obstacle is his own, and it is expensive to maintain, since the money that keeps him free belongs to his family.

The courtship is also a proposal about how a woman with twin daughters and no husband is going to live, and she knows it. In nineteen-sixties Argentina the man doing the courting is older, courteous, and not fully accounted for, and Ariel Rotter gives most of ninety-five minutes to her side of the arrangement rather than his. She is not being hurried anywhere. She is weighing, and the weighing is not a failure of feeling. A household is on offer, along with a name for it and an end to doing the sums alone. The audience prize at IFFR went to it. Period pictures generally want the past as costume; this one wants the calculation a widow was expected to make, and the short interval she was given before somebody else made it for her.
